blocks.text: A 16-year-old athlete collapses during a school cross-country run. In the emergency department her pulse is 38 beats per minute, her hands and feet are cold, and fine downy hair covers her forearms. She insists she is 'fine' and 'just needs to lose a little more'. A heart rate that low would alarm you in anyone; in a young person who looks well to her family, it can signal a disorder with one of the highest mortality rates in psychiatry.

blocks.markdown: Psychiatric disorders present differently across the life course. This unit covers three groups: the **neurodevelopmental conditions** attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism; the **perinatal mental illnesses** (perinatal depression and puerperal psychosis); and **anorexia nervosa**, a psychiatric disorder with major physical consequences. In each, a careful developmental or physical assessment matters as much as the mental state.

blocks.title: Neurodevelopmental disorder
blocks.text: A neurodevelopmental disorder arises from atypical brain development, presents in early life, and causes persistent functional difficulties. ADHD and autism are common examples; both are highly heritable and may coexist.

blocks.markdown:
### ADHD and autism

**ADHD** is a persistent pattern of **inattention** (distractibility, losing things, not finishing tasks, difficulty organising) and/or **hyperactivity-impulsivity** (fidgeting, difficulty remaining seated, talking excessively, interrupting, acting without thinking). DSM-5 requires several symptoms present before about age 12, in **two or more settings** (for example home and school), with clear impairment that is not better explained by another disorder. Presentations are predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, or combined. Comorbidity is common (oppositional defiant and conduct disorder, anxiety, learning and language difficulties, tic disorders, autism). Assessment includes developmental history, informant reports from parents and teachers, observation, rating scales and exclusion of other causes (hearing or vision problems, sleep disorders, thyroid disease, anxiety, trauma, medication effects).

**Management** combines psychoeducation, parent training and school adjustments with medication when symptoms remain impairing. In UK guidance a stimulant such as **methylphenidate** is commonly the first-line drug for school-age children; other options include lisdexamfetamine, atomoxetine and guanfacine. Monitor **height, weight, blood pressure, pulse, appetite, sleep and tics**, and check doses and indications in the current BNF and NICE guidance.

**Autism** is defined by persistent deficits in **social communication and social interaction** (reduced reciprocity, atypical eye contact and gesture, difficulty developing relationships) together with **restricted, repetitive patterns** of behaviour, interests or activities (stereotyped movements, insistence on sameness and routine, intense focused interests, sensory hypo- or hypersensitivity). Symptoms begin in the early developmental period, though may become evident later when social demands rise. Assessment is multidisciplinary and developmental, with hearing assessment and consideration of language disorder, learning disability and genetic conditions. There is no drug treatment for the core features; support is educational and behavioural, with treatment of coexisting anxiety, ADHD, epilepsy and sleep problems.

rows: Social communication deficit plus restricted, repetitive behaviours
Primary difficulty with reciprocity and reading social cues
Constant movement, difficulty waiting, short attention
Limited joint attention and pointing, atypical play, distress at change
Parent training, school support, stimulant medication where indicated
Social communication support, environmental adaptation, treat comorbidity; no drug for core features
May coexist with ADHD, anxiety, epilepsy and learning disability

blocks.markdown:
### Perinatal mental illness

The perinatal period (pregnancy to the first postnatal year) is a time of high risk for mental illness. Three distinct postnatal conditions are recognised.

**Baby blues** are transient tearfulness, lability and anxiety, typically starting around the third to fifth day after birth and resolving within about two weeks, affecting a large proportion of mothers. They need reassurance and support only.

**Perinatal (postnatal) depression** affects roughly one in ten women, with onset usually within the first weeks to months, although it may begin in pregnancy. Features are as for depression (low mood, anhedonia, sleep and appetite change, guilt, loss of energy) with anxiety about the baby and difficulty bonding. Screening uses the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**, a ten-item scale scored 0 to 3 per item (total 0 to 30), with a commonly used threshold of around 13 for probable depression (thresholds vary); the final item concerns thoughts of self-harm, and any positive response needs prompt clinical assessment. Treatment depends on severity: psychological therapy, and an antidepressant when indicated, with careful risk-benefit review of drugs in pregnancy and breastfeeding using the BNF and specialist advice. For example, **valproate** carries a high risk of major congenital malformations and neurodevelopmental disorders after exposure in pregnancy; the MHRA advises that it must not be used in girls and women of childbearing potential unless other treatments are ineffective or not tolerated and the conditions of the Pregnancy Prevention Programme are met (check current MHRA guidance and the BNF).

**Puerperal (postpartum) psychosis** is a psychiatric emergency affecting around 1 to 2 per 1000 births. Onset is rapid, typically within the first two weeks after delivery: insomnia, elated or labile mood, confusion, perplexity, delusions (often about the baby) and hallucinations. The strongest risk factors are a past or family history of **bipolar disorder** or of puerperal psychosis. There is a risk of suicide and of harm to the infant. Management is urgent psychiatric assessment and, usually, **admission, ideally to a specialist mother-and-baby unit**, with antipsychotic or mood-stabilising treatment (and sometimes ECT), after excluding organic causes such as infection, thyroid disease or delirium.

blocks.caption: Postnatal mood disorders
rows: Tearful, labile, resolves within about 2 weeks
Weeks to months (may start in pregnancy)
Low mood, anhedonia, anxiety, impaired bonding
Screening, psychological therapy, antidepressant if indicated
Rapid onset mood disturbance, delusions, hallucinations, confusion, insomnia
Emergency psychiatric admission, ideally to a mother-and-baby unit

blocks.title: Scoring and interpreting an EPDS
blocks.prompt: At the eight-week postnatal check a woman completes the EPDS. Her ten item scores (each 0 to 3, already adjusted for reverse-scored items) are 2, 1, 2, 0, 3, 2, 1, 1, 2, 0. Item 10 (thoughts of self-harm) scored 0. Calculate the total and interpret it.

steps.text: Check the maximum: 10 items x 3 points = 30.
Compare with the commonly used threshold of about 13: a score of 14 is above it and suggests possible depression, although the cut-off varies between settings.

Take the next steps: item 10 is zero, but ask directly about mood, sleep, bonding, anxiety and risk, and arrange a clinical assessment. The score screens; it does not diagnose, so confirm with an interview and exclude causes such as anaemia and thyroid dysfunction.

blocks.answer: EPDS = 14, above the usual screening threshold, requiring clinical assessment for perinatal depression.

blocks.markdown:
### Anorexia nervosa

**Anorexia nervosa** is characterised by restriction of energy intake leading to a significantly low body weight, an intense fear of gaining weight or persistent behaviour that prevents weight gain, and disturbance in the experience of body weight or shape (or an undue influence of weight on self-evaluation, or lack of recognition of the seriousness of the low weight). Subtypes are **restricting** and **binge-eating/purging**. It usually begins in adolescence, is more common in girls and women, and carries high mortality from physical complications and suicide.

**Assessment** is both psychiatric and physical. Take a history of eating, weight change, exercise, purging, laxative, diuretic and diet pill use, menstrual history and body image; assess mood, self-harm and suicide risk, and comorbidity (depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive features). Examine for **low BMI, bradycardia, hypotension (including postural), hypothermia, cold peripheries, lanugo, dependent oedema and proximal muscle weakness** (for example the sit-up-squat-stand test). Investigate with electrolytes (including potassium, magnesium, phosphate, sodium), glucose, urea and creatinine, liver function, full blood count, calcium, ECG (bradycardia and QT interval), and consider bone density assessment in prolonged illness. Specific thresholds for admission are set in current guidance (for example the Royal College of Psychiatrists guidance on medical emergencies in eating disorders), so consult that source.

**Medical risks** include arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death (bradycardia, QT prolongation, electrolyte disturbance, especially hypokalaemia with purging), hypoglycaemia, **osteopenia and osteoporosis**, amenorrhoea and infertility, growth and pubertal delay in adolescents, constipation and delayed gastric emptying, leukopenia and anaemia, and **refeeding syndrome**, a potentially fatal shift in fluid and electrolytes (hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, sodium and fluid retention, cardiac failure, Wernicke encephalopathy) upon restarting nutrition. Refeeding is therefore carried out cautiously with monitoring and thiamine supplementation per local protocol.

**Treatment** is specialist and multidisciplinary: family-based treatment for adolescents, and eating-disorder-focused psychological therapy (such as CBT-ED, MANTRA or specialist supportive clinical management) for adults, with medical monitoring, nutritional rehabilitation and admission when medically unstable. No drug has a first-line role for the core illness. Treatment may be given under mental health law when a patient lacks capacity or is at serious risk.

blocks.caption: Body mass index: mass m in kilograms, height h in metres, result in kg/m^2. In children and adolescents it is interpreted against age- and sex-specific centiles.

blocks.title: Calculating BMI and recognising red flags
blocks.prompt: A 24-year-old woman with a two-year history of restrictive eating weighs 44 kg and is 1.65 m tall. Her pulse is 42 beats per minute, her blood pressure is low on standing, and she reports amenorrhoea for 14 months. Calculate her BMI and decide what the findings imply for management.

steps.text: Divide the mass by this value.

Interpret: the BMI is markedly low for an adult, and the bradycardia, postural hypotension and prolonged amenorrhoea reflect physical compromise. These indicate medical risk that needs urgent evaluation.

Act: obtain electrolytes, glucose, ECG and a medical review, check for specific admission criteria in current guidance and local protocol, and refer urgently to a specialist eating disorder service. Plan any refeeding carefully with electrolyte monitoring and thiamine.

blocks.answer: BMI is about 16.2 kg/m^2, with physical red flags requiring urgent medical assessment, ECG and bloods, and specialist referral, with a cautious refeeding plan.

blocks.title: Do not be falsely reassured
blocks.text: Normal bloods do not exclude serious risk in anorexia nervosa. Electrolytes, glucose and BMI are insensitive to imminent cardiac and metabolic deterioration, so pulse, blood pressure, temperature, ECG and muscle strength matter. Check thresholds and regimens against current guidance, the BNF and local policy.

points: ADHD (inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity in two or more settings, onset in childhood) and autism (social communication deficit plus restricted, repetitive behaviour) are neurodevelopmental conditions that may coexist; ADHD medication needs growth and cardiovascular monitoring.

Baby blues are brief and benign, perinatal depression is common and screened by tools such as the EPDS, and puerperal psychosis is a rare emergency linked to bipolar disorder that needs urgent admission, ideally to a mother-and-baby unit.

Anorexia nervosa assessment combines psychiatric and physical examination (BMI, pulse, blood pressure, ECG, electrolytes); its medical risks include arrhythmia, osteoporosis, infertility and refeeding syndrome.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy is referred because he cannot stay seated in class, calls out answers, loses his belongings and is described similarly by his parents at home. Which additional feature is required to support a diagnosis of ADHD?

options.text: Symptoms present in at least two settings with onset in childhood and clear functional impairment
Symptoms present only at school
Onset after the age of 25
Normal behaviour when observed in clinic, with no impairment

questions.correctOptionText: Symptoms present in at least two settings with onset in childhood and clear functional impairment

distractorRationale.a: Correct: pervasiveness across settings, early onset and impairment are required.
distractorRationale.b: Symptoms confined to one setting suggest a situational problem.
distractorRationale.c: ADHD begins in childhood, not after 25.
distractorRationale.d: Impairment is required, and clinic observation can be unreliable.

questions.explanation: ADHD requires symptoms across more than one setting, onset in childhood (before about age 12) and impairment, to distinguish it from a response to one difficult environment. Informants from home and school are therefore essential.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl does not point to show things to her parents, rarely looks at faces when called, lines up her toy cars repeatedly and becomes extremely distressed if the route to nursery changes. Her hearing test is normal. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: The pattern of impaired social communication with repetitive behaviour and resistance to change suggests autism and warrants multidisciplinary assessment
This is typical normal development at this age
Immunisation is the likely cause and should be investigated first
A stimulant should be started to treat the core features

questions.correctOptionText: The pattern of impaired social communication with repetitive behaviour and resistance to change suggests autism and warrants multidisciplinary assessment

distractorRationale.a: Correct: both diagnostic domains are present and hearing loss has been excluded.
distractorRationale.b: Absent joint attention and ritualistic behaviour are not typical.
distractorRationale.d: No drug treats the core features of autism.

questions.explanation: Autism is characterised by social communication deficits and restricted, repetitive behaviours with insistence on sameness, with onset in early childhood. Normal hearing helps exclude one differential, and assessment is multidisciplinary with no drug treatment for core features.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy with ADHD has started methylphenidate. Which monitoring plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Regular height, weight, blood pressure, pulse, appetite, sleep and tic assessment, with dose checked against current BNF and NICE guidance
Monthly liver biopsy
Lithium levels every month
No monitoring is required for stimulants

questions.correctOptionText: Regular height, weight, blood pressure, pulse, appetite, sleep and tic assessment, with dose checked against current BNF and NICE guidance

distractorRationale.a: Correct: stimulants affect appetite, growth, cardiovascular parameters and sleep.
distractorRationale.c: Lithium is not used or relevant here.

questions.explanation: Stimulants can suppress appetite and growth and raise heart rate and blood pressure, and may worsen sleep or tics. Regular monitoring of these parameters is therefore standard, with the schedule taken from current guidance.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman, 9 days after the birth of her first baby, has hardly slept for three nights. She is elated, talks rapidly, seems perplexed and tells her husband that the baby has been sent to test her. She has a history of bipolar disorder. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Urgent psychiatric assessment and admission, ideally to a specialist mother-and-baby unit, after excluding organic causes
Reassurance that this is baby blues and will pass
Routine outpatient review in six weeks
Start a long-term benzodiazepine alone and send her home

questions.correctOptionText: Urgent psychiatric assessment and admission, ideally to a specialist mother-and-baby unit, after excluding organic causes

distractorRationale.a: Correct: rapid-onset psychosis in the first weeks after delivery is an emergency.
distractorRationale.b: Baby blues are mild and do not cause delusions or marked insomnia.
distractorRationale.c: Delay is dangerous given suicide and infant risk.
distractorRationale.d: A benzodiazepine alone does not treat psychosis and sending her home is unsafe.

questions.explanation: Rapid-onset elated mood, insomnia, perplexity and delusions within days of delivery, in a woman with bipolar disorder, indicate puerperal psychosis. It is a psychiatric emergency because of risks to mother and infant, and admission to a mother-and-baby unit is preferred.

questions.stem: True or false: Postnatal 'baby blues', which begin around days 3 to 5 and settle within about two weeks, require routine antidepressant treatment.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Baby blues are common, short-lived and self-limiting, and management is reassurance and support. Persistence beyond about two weeks or severe symptoms should prompt assessment for perinatal depression.

questions.stem: A woman completes the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (10 items, each scored 0 to 3, already adjusted for reverse scoring). Her item scores are 0, 1, 1, 2, 0, 1, 0, 1, 2, 0. Calculate her total EPDS score (units: points).
questions.explanation: The total is 0 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 2 + 0 = 8 out of 30. This lies below the commonly used threshold of about 13, but a screening score does not exclude depression, and clinical concern or any self-harm response would still prompt assessment.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman with severe anorexia nervosa, who has eaten almost nothing for more than a week, is admitted and nutrition is restarted. Five days later she develops breathlessness, peripheral oedema and confusion, and her blood tests show low phosphate, potassium and magnesium. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.text: Refeeding syndrome
Puerperal psychosis
Serotonin syndrome
Alcohol withdrawal

distractorRationale.a: Correct: electrolyte shifts and fluid retention after restarting nutrition in a starved patient.
distractorRationale.b: Unrelated to nutrition and not postpartum.
distractorRationale.d: No alcohol history and electrolytes pattern points elsewhere.

questions.explanation: Reintroducing carbohydrate stimulates insulin, driving phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells, and causing fluid retention, which can lead to cardiac failure and Wernicke encephalopathy. Slow reintroduction, electrolyte monitoring, replacement and thiamine are therefore routine.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with suspected anorexia nervosa weighs 41 kg and is 1.62 m tall. Calculate her body mass index (units: kg/m^2), to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: BMI = mass divided by height squared: 1.62 x 1.62 = 2.6244, and 41 / 2.6244 = 15.62, which rounds to 15.6 kg/m^2. This is markedly low, but risk assessment also depends on pulse, blood pressure, ECG, electrolytes and the rate of weight loss.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl is brought by her mother after losing weight over a year. She exercises daily, avoids family meals and says she is fat. Outline your assessment, including the physical examination and investigations, and explain why she may be at serious medical risk even if she looks well.
markingGuide: History of eating, weight change, exercise, purging, laxatives and menstrual history; body image and fear of weight gain
Psychiatric assessment including mood, self-harm and suicide risk, with parental and collateral information
Weight, height and BMI (adolescent centiles), pulse, blood pressure (lying and standing), temperature
Examination for lanugo, cold peripheries, oedema and muscle weakness (sit-up-squat-stand test)
Investigations: electrolytes including potassium, magnesium and phosphate, glucose, renal and liver function, full blood count, ECG
Medical risks: bradycardia, arrhythmia and sudden death, hypoglycaemia, electrolyte disturbance, osteoporosis, amenorrhoea and growth impairment
Appearances and normal blood tests can be falsely reassuring
Mention of specialist referral, family-based treatment and current guidance on admission thresholds
questions.explanation: A good assessment covers psychiatric features, risk and a focused physical examination with ECG and bloods. Young people can compensate until the point of sudden decompensation, so vital signs and ECG matter more than appearance.

questions.stem: Compare baby blues, perinatal depression and puerperal psychosis in terms of timing, presentation and management, and explain why screening for a history of bipolar disorder is part of antenatal care.
markingGuide: Baby blues: days 3 to 5, transient tearfulness, resolves within about two weeks, support only
Perinatal depression: weeks to months, low mood, anhedonia, anxiety and impaired bonding; screening (EPDS), psychological therapy, antidepressant if indicated with risk-benefit review

Puerperal psychosis: rapid onset usually within two weeks, insomnia, mood elevation or lability, delusions and hallucinations, confusion; an emergency needing admission, ideally to a mother-and-baby unit, and antipsychotic or mood-stabilising treatment, ECT in some cases
Past or family history of bipolar disorder or puerperal psychosis is the strongest risk factor, so identifying it allows planning and prophylaxis
Exclude organic causes such as infection or thyroid disease
Drugs in pregnancy or breastfeeding need specialist and BNF review, noting avoidance of valproate in women who may become pregnant
questions.explanation: The three conditions differ in onset, severity and urgency, which guides management. Past bipolar disorder greatly increases the risk of puerperal psychosis, so identifying it antenatally allows a preventive plan and early monitoring after delivery.
